title: Payments slow right after release
executive_summary: INC-005 (SEV1): Payment and order latency degraded from about 11:40Z, shortly after the payment-service 5.8.0 release (11:32Z). The investigation status is ROOT_CAUSE_IDENTIFIED, and the leading explanation is the most probable cause, not a confirmed fact: storage/WAL I/O degradation on the postgres volume vol-0a3f. Volume write latency rose (avg ~835 ms) from 11:21Z (logpat-postgres-d629c24d), and checkpoints slowed to ~450 s with WAL write errors from 11:24Z (logpat-postgres-7ce84fae). A disk I/O wait step at about 11:22Z precedes the rest of the chain (critic summary). Postgres p95 rose from 11:23Z (met-postgres-p95_latency_ms-1110-1205), and connection utilisation climbed from 11:26Z to a window mean of ~74% (max ~96%). Payment-service charges.insert statements then exceeded the 2000 ms timeout from 11:28:17Z (logpat-payment-service-c828e437). Payment p95 rose from 11:27Z (baseline ~150 ms to a mean of ~1155 ms) and user-service and auth-service followed the same pattern on the postgres path. Postgres CPU fell, which fits I/O wait rather than compute saturation. The deployment hypothesis (H2) is rejected because the anomalies started before the release, and the payment CPU and request rate are unchanged. The report_rollup() hypothesis (H3) is rejected as the primary cause because its slow queries began after the storage degradation. It may still have amplified connection hold time.

critic_review.summary: Leading hypothesis H1 (storage/WAL I/O degradation on the postgres volume vol-0a3f) is well supported and consistent in time. Postgres disk_io_wait_ms, previously only log-inferred, now shows a metric step at 11:22Z (baseline 2.0 ms, window ~107 ms mean, ~130-157 ms through 12:05Z), which precedes postgres p95 (11:23Z), connection utilisation (11:26Z), payment p95 (11:27Z) and payment error_rate (11:28Z). Storage warnings (11:21Z) and checkpoint/WAL errors (11:24Z) corroborate. Postgres CPU fell, consistent with I/O wait rather than compute. Auth-service is flat, and user-service shows the same tail pattern on the postgres path. H2 is rejected: its cause time (11:32Z) is after anomalies began at 11:21-11:27Z, payment CPU/request rate are unchanged, and user-service (not on 5.8.0) shows the same degradation. H3 is rejected as the primary cause: report_rollup() slow queries begin at 11:28Z, after the storage degradation at 11:21Z. It may be a secondary amplifier of connection hold time, but it does not explain onset. Caveat: payment-service timeout_rate is flat (~0.1%) even though charges.insert timeout errors are logged, so the measurement layer for timeouts is unclear; the error_rate step does confirm user-facing failures. Root-cause category is storage degradation on the postgres culprit; the underlying cloud-side trigger for the volume is out of scope.

assessments.reasoning: Disk I/O wait metric step at 11:22Z precedes all downstream anomalies. Corroborated by storage and checkpoint/WAL logs, postgres p95 and connection utilisation onset, and the tail-only pattern on payment and user services. Unaffected auth/redis paths localise the fault. Timeout_rate flatness is a minor measurement inconsistency, not a refutation.
Cause time 11:32Z postdates anomaly onsets at 11:21-11:27Z. Payment CPU, memory and request rate are unchanged. user-service, which does not run 5.8.0, shows the same degradation.

report_rollup() slowness starts at 11:28Z, after storage degradation (11:21Z) and checkpoint slowness (11:24Z). It cannot be the initiating cause. It may be a secondary contributor to connection pressure, which can be noted without changing the primary category.

root_cause_statement: ROOT CAUSE IDENTIFIED (critic-approved; still an INFERENCE from evidence): infrastructure_degradation in postgres - Storage/WAL I/O degradation on the postgres volume vol-0a3f slowed writes and checkpoints, which backed up connections and caused charges.insert statement timeouts and tail latency on payment-service and order-service.
corrective_actions: Mitigate the degraded postgres storage now: fail over or move the database to a healthy volume or replica, or restore I/O capacity on vol-0a3f (cloud-side investigation is outside this report's scope) (logpat-postgres-d629c24d, met-postgres-p95_latency_ms-1110-1205).
Temporarily pause or throttle report_rollup() on the primary database to reduce I/O and connection hold time while storage is degraded (logpat-postgres-44883ca5, secondary amplifier only).

Reduce payment-service and order-service DB pool wait pressure, for example by shedding non-critical load or tuning pool limits, until postgres latency recovers (met-payment-service-db_conn_util_pct-1030-1230).

Do not roll back payment-service 5.8.0 as the primary fix, since H2 is rejected. A rollback could still be considered only if storage recovery does not restore latency and the team wants to rule it out (dep-31448d11).
preventive_actions: Add storage health monitoring and alerting for database volumes (write latency, I/O wait, checkpoint duration) with paging thresholds set before the latency reaches user-facing levels.
Review the postgres volume type and provisioned I/O capacity against peak write and checkpoint load, and set checkpoint and WAL tuning accordingly.
Schedule heavy reporting jobs such as report_rollup() away from the primary during peak hours, or move them to a replica.

Verify the payment-service to postgres dependency path and confirm the charges.insert timeout instrumentation, since the timeout metric was flat even though timeout errors were logged (logpat-payment-service-c828e437).
monitoring_recommendations: Alert on postgres volume write latency above 100 ms and disk_io_wait_ms above a baseline of ~2 ms sustained for 2 minutes (met-postgres-p95_latency_ms-1110-1205; disk I/O step at ~11:22Z).
Alert on postgres checkpoint duration above 60 s and on any 'WAL write slow' error log (logpat-postgres-7ce84fae).
Alert on postgres db_conn_util_pct above 70% sustained, and on payment-service db_conn_util_pct above 60% (met-postgres-db_conn_util_pct-1110-1205, met-payment-service-db_conn_util_pct-1030-1230).
Alert on payment-service charges.insert statement timeouts and fix the timeout_rate metric so it reflects logged timeout errors (logpat-payment-service-c828e437).
Track p95 latency for payment-service, order-service, and user-service against baseline (~150 ms, ~80 ms) with a dashboard that shows the postgres path alongside them.
limitations: The cloud-side root trigger for the vol-0a3f degradation was not investigated.
The payment-service timeout_rate metric stayed flat (~0.1%) even though charges.insert timeout errors were logged, so the timeout measurement layer is unreliable.
The payment-service to postgres dependency for charges.insert is inferred, not explicitly confirmed.
The I/O contribution from report_rollup() was not quantified, so its secondary effect cannot be ruled out in size.
Confidence values are rule-based evidence-strength scores, not calibrated probabilities.
Investigation terminated because: critic verdict APPROVED
conclusion: INC-005 is most probably caused by storage and WAL I/O degradation on the postgres volume vol-0a3f, which slowed writes and checkpoints, exhausted database connections, and drove charges.insert timeouts and tail latency in payment-service, order-service, and user-service. The release of payment-service 5.8.0 is not the cause (H2 rejected), and report_rollup() is at most a secondary amplifier (H3 rejected as primary). The confidence is 0.88. The measurement of timeouts is unclear, since the timeout_rate metric is flat despite logged timeout errors. The cloud-side trigger for the volume degradation is outside this investigation's scope. Immediate work should focus on restoring database storage health, and the monitoring above should be in place before the next release.
